## Mac users
Almost everything here works the same in the Mac Terminal. The exceptions are small: the Linux commands `free` and `nproc` don't exist on a Mac (use `top`, and `sysctl -n hw.ncpu`), `ps aux --sort=...` and `stat -c` are Linux-only forms, and the shell's startup file is `~/.zshrc` instead of `~/.bashrc`.
:::

The file system is a tree. You  (via the linux prompt) are always "in" one directory, called the **working directory**. Let's verify we are in the right directory using `pwd` (print [the] working directory).

# Download data

We will start with `covid.csv`, from the New York Times' public repository of COVID-19 data. The file tracks COVID-19 in the United States during 2020: each row gives one county on one day, with the total cases and deaths reported there up to that day. It has about 885,000 rows and takes about 35 MB.

Our first "real" linux command is `curl` (client URL) which downloads whatever is at the web address (a URL) you supply. 

```bash
curl -L -o covid.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nytimes/covid-19-data/master/us-counties-2020.csv
#^^^  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^^^^^^^
#  |  cmd options    cmd argument
# linux command
```

A command has three parts: the **command** itself, **options** (also called flags) that change its behavior, and **arguments** that tell it what to act on.

We gave it two options:

- `-L` follows redirects: if the server says the file has moved, `curl` automatically fetches it from the new location.
- `-o covid.csv` saves the download in a file with that name. Without `-o`, `curl` prints the contents to the screen.

You don't have to memorize options like these. Almost every command comes with a manual page that lists them, which you open with `man`:

```bash
man curl      # the full manual page (type /--output to search, q to quit)
curl --help   # a shorter summary (GNU/Linux tools)
```


Now let's make sure the `curl` actually worked i.e. downloaded the website and named it correctly. For this we'll use our next command `ls` (list [contents of a directory]). We will use a few options

```bash
ls
ls -l           #list with "l"ong details
ls -l -h        #+ list with "h"uman readable file sizes
ls -l -h -a     #+ list "a"ll including hidden files
ls -lha         #`ls -lha` is the same as `ls -l -h -a` this is my go-to 
ls -lhaS        #my other go-to as it also sorts by size
```

The . and .. are "hidden" and signify special directory entries known as "hard links" that act as shortcuts for file system navigation. The `.` is the current directory. We will use it soon. The `..` is the parent directory e.g.

```bash
cd .    #does nothing as it's changing directory into the current directory
pwd
cd ..   #visit one directory up
pwd
```

An **absolute path** starts from the root, `/` so the following will fail

```bash
cd /lec01
```

This fails because there is no `lec01` directory in the root:

```bash
ls /
```

The following is the listing of all files and directories from the root. If you're a sysadmin, you'll be using logs in the root folder `var` a lot and installing programs to `bin` and `opt`. But this is not a class in linux sysadmin - we only need to know what's useful for the data world.

A **relative path** starts from where you are i.e. beginning with pwd. So

```bash
cd lec01
```

is short for

```bash
cd /home/kapelner/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec01
#  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
#  this is the current working directory 
```

Text file stats via `wc` (word count)

```bash
wc -l covid.csv                # count the number of lines in the file
wc -lwmc covid.csv             # count the number of lines, words, characters, bytes in the file
```


Keyboard habits that save hours:

| Key | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| Ctrl+L or `clear` | Clear the screen |
| Tab | Completes file and command names e.g. wc co<tab> Press twice to see options. |
| ↑ / ↓ | Scroll through previous commands |
| Ctrl+R | Search your command history (Enter to run, Ctrl+R again to get previous, Ctrl+G to clear) |
| Ctrl+C | Stop the running command |
| Ctrl+U | Clear the line |

```bash
history             # list your recent commands
which python3       # where is this program installed?
echo $HOME          # print a variable: your home directory (what "~" means)
echo $PATH          # the directories searched for programs
echo $PATH | grep "bigdata" #we will see what this means later
```

The PATH variable is pretty important. You will be adding directories to it for convenience at times so you don't need to specify absolute path each time you want to run a new program you installed.

# Managing files

```bash
touch notes.txt             # create an empty file (or update its timestamp)
ls -alhS
cp notes.txt notes2.txt     # copy a file
ls -alhS
mkdir tmp_dir               # make a directory (we've seen this before)
ls -alhS
cp -r tmp_dir tmp_dir_copy  # copy a directory (-r = recursive)
ls -alhS
mv notes2.txt tmp_dir/      # move a file to another folder
ls -alhS
ls tmp_dir/ -alhS
mv tmp_dir/notes2.txt .     # move it to the working directory (that `.`!)
ls -alhS
mv notes.txt my_notes.txt   # rename (via moving to a new name)
ls -alhS
rm notes.txt                # delete a file
ls -alhS
rm notes2.txt my_notes.txt  # delete multiple files
rm -r tmp_dir               # delete a directory and everything in it (r is for "recursive" which is needed)
ls -alhS
rm tmp_dir_copy             # fails
rm -r tmp_dir_copy 
ls -alhS
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## There is no trash can in the linux shell
`rm` deletes permanently. There is no undo.
:::

**Wildcards.** Often you want a command to act on many files at once: every `.csv` file, or every file whose name starts with `file_`. Instead of typing each name, you type a **pattern**, a short description of the names you mean, and the shell works out which files match. Pattern languages turn up everywhere in data work. The shell's version, called **wildcards** or **globs**, has just three building blocks: `*`, `?` and `[...]`. Later in this lecture, `grep` will search *inside* files using a richer pattern language called **regular expressions**. The two look alike and are easy to confuse: in a wildcard `*` means "any characters", while in a regular expression it means "repeat the previous thing any number of times". For now, wildcards:

```bash
touch tmp.csv file_1.txt file_2.txt file_10.tex   # touch takes several names
ls *.csv            # * matches any run of characters, including none
ls file_?.txt       # ? matches exactly one character: file_1.txt, not file_10
ls file_[12].txt    # [...] matches one character from the set
ls file_[0-9].*     # ranges work too plus other wildcards (the suffix can be anything)
ls file_[!1]*       # [!...] matches one character NOT in the set
ls *_1*             # wildcards can go anywhere in the name
ls file_{1,10}.*    # {a,b} is not a wildcard: the shell writes out both names
echo file_{1,10}.*  # see what a pattern expands to before using it with rm
```

The shell expands a pattern into the matching names *before* the command runs, so `ls *.csv` is really `ls covid.csv tmp.csv`, and `ls *` alone lists the contents of every subdirectory too. Patterns never match names that start with a dot (hidden files) unless you write the dot yourself.

**Finding files:** `find` walks a directory tree and prints every file that passes the tests you give it. The first argument is where to start; everything after it is a test.

```bash
find . -name "*.csv"        # find CSV files in the working directory and its subdirectories
find ~ -name "*.csv"        # all csv files anywhere under my home directory and its subdirectories
                            # (your list will differ; I have a lot of files in my WSL as I use it for all my projects)
find . -type f              # only files...
find . -type d              # ...or only directories
find ~ -maxdepth 1 -type f  # don't descend into subdirectories
find . -size +10M           # files bigger than 10 MB
find . -size -1k            # files smaller than 1 KB (the ones we touched)
find . -empty               # empty files and directories
find . -mmin -30            # modified in the last 30 minutes
find . -mtime +7            # modified more than 7 days ago
find . -newer covid.csv     # modified after covid.csv was
```

Several tests in a row must all hold. Use `-o` for "or" and `-not` to negate:

```bash
find . -type f -name "*.csv" -size +1M    # all three must hold
find . -name "*.csv" -o -name "*.tex"     # either suffix
find . -type f -not -name "*.csv"         # everything except csv files
```

Once `find` has the files, it can do something with them. `-exec` runs a command on each result, with `{}` standing for the file name:

```bash
find . -name "*.txt" -delete              # delete every match (no confirmation given)
ls -alhS
rm -i *.tex                               # ask before each deletion
```

Searching from `/` reaches directories you are not allowed to read, which produces error messages.

```bash
find / -name "*.csv*"
```

Every program has two separate output channels:

- stdout (channel 1) carries normal results, such as the file names find prints.
- stderr (channel 2) carries error messages, such as "find: '...': Permission denied."

Both go to your screen by default, so they look the same. They are separate streams, though, and the program chooses which one to write each line to. find writes matches to stdout and complaints to stderr. So we want to filter out the errors

```bash
find / -name "*.csv*" 2>/dev/null   # no more clutter from looking at useless directories
```

In 2>/dev/null, the 2> means "redirect channel 2 somewhere else", and /dev/null is a special file that throws away anything written to it. Everything on channel 2 is discarded, and channel 1 is untouched.


**Redirects.** A **redirect** sends a command's input or output somewhere other than the keyboard and screen. The symbols are `>` (send output to a file), `>>` (add output to the end of a file), `2>` (send the error channel to a file) and `<` (read input from a file). The command itself doesn't change, only where its output goes:

```bash
echo "hello"                 # prints hello on the screen
echo "hello" > notes.txt     # redirect into a file so nothing printed to terminal because it went into notes.txt
ls -alh
cat notes.txt                # cat is "concatenate" which is used mostly to not concatenate but print to screen instead
echo "again" >> notes.txt    # >> adds the object of redirection to a new line at the end (i.e. "new line append")
wc -l notes.txt
cat notes.txt
echo "oops" > notes.txt      # > replaces the contents: no warning!
cat notes.txt 
```

Redirects work with any command, and a redirected file is created if it doesn't exist:

```bash
ls > listing.txt             # save a directory listing
cat listing.txt
date > today.txt             # save the current date and time
cat today.txt
cat notes.txt notes.txt > twice.txt   # join files into a new file (the original intent of the cat command)
cat twice.txt
ls /nonexistent
ls /nonexistent > err.txt   #can we redirect this output?
cat err.txt                 #no, because redirect by default is stdout, not stderr, it's short for 1>
ls /nonexistent 2> err.txt   # save the error message instead of showing it
cat err.txt
ls . /nonexistent
ls . /nonexistent > out.txt
cat out.txt
ls . /nonexistent 1> out.txt
cat out.txt
ls . /nonexistent 1> out.txt 2> err.txt      # results and errors in two different files
cat out.txt
cat err.txt
ls . /nonexistent > all.txt 2>&1      # results and errors in one file the &1 says direct to where 1 went
cat all.txt
```

**A first shell script.** A shell script is a text file of commands that the shell runs one after another, so a sequence you would otherwise retype can be saved and rerun. Here is the smallest useful one: a file `my_script.sh` with a single line, `touch file1.txt`, which creates an empty file.

```bash
echo "touch file1.txt" > my_script.sh   # sh is the standard extension for "shell script"
                                        # although it is not necessary to name it so, it's a good convention though
cat my_script.sh                        # touch file1.txt
ls -alhS                                # file1.txt doesn't exist yet
```

Now let's run this script by giving it to "bash" (Bourne Again SHell). Each line must be either (a) a valid Linux command or (b) a bash command which is a small programming language itself. 

```bash
bash my_script.sh 
ls -alhS
```

A script can contain commands like ls and grep, and also bash syntax: variables (name="Ada"), if/for/while, &&, $(...), functions and comments. Those aren't separate programs. They are part of bash itself. 






./my_script.sh                          # error: Permission denied (see below)

The last line fails because the file is not marked as something the computer may run. That is what permissions control, and we fix it next. (We write a more useful script later in this lecture.)

**Permissions.** In the output of `ls -l`, the first column looks like `-rwxr-xr--`: read, write, and execute permissions for the owner, the group, and everyone else.

```bash
ls -lha
chmod +x my_script.sh   # make it executable: ./my_script.sh now works
sudo apt install htop   # run one command as administrator
```

`sudo` asks for your Linux password. Use it only when a command needs it, typically for installing software.

# Editing in the terminal

On a remote server there is no graphical editor, so you need to be able to edit a file in the terminal. The two common terminal editors are `vi` and `nano`. We will only use `vi`; you can learn `nano` on your own.

::: {.callout-note}
## Which is used more, vi or nano?
Vi, by about two to one. In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 24.3% of developers said they use Vim and 12.2% use Nano. Another 14% use Neovim, a modern rewrite of Vim, so the vi family together is ahead by more than three to one. Also, you can count on finding vi. It's installed on virtually every Unix system, including bare servers and containers where nothing else is installed.
:::

However, it has a learning curve. It has **modes**, which is what confuses everyone at first.

```bash
vi notes.txt
```

The survival kit:

| Keys | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `i` | Enter insert mode: now you can type |
| Esc | Leave insert mode |
| `:set nu` +Enter | Add line numbers |
| `:777` +Enter | Go to line #777 |
| `:w` +Enter | Save |
| `:q` +Enter | Quit |
| `:wq` +Enter | Save and quit |
| `:q!` +Enter | Quit **without** saving |
| `/word` +Enter | Search for "word" (`n` for next match) |
| `d3` | Delete 3 lines |
| `u` | Undo |

If you're ever stuck in `vi`, press Esc a few times, then type `:q!` and Enter.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Practice later
`vimtutor` is a 30-minute interactive vi tutorial. On Ubuntu, install it with `sudo apt install vim`.
:::

# Looking at data without opening it

This is the most important section for big data. A file can be far larger than what you want to (or can) load into memory, but you can still look at it.

We will now return to our downloaded file. The columns are `date`, `county`, `state`, `fips` (a numeric code for the county), `cases` and `deaths`. Source: The New York Times, based on reports from state and local health agencies, <https://github.com/nytimes/covid-19-data>.

```bash
cat covid.csv         # print the whole file (bad idea for big files!)
less covid.csv        # scroll through a file (q quits, / searches)
head covid.csv        # first 10 lines
head -n 3 covid.csv   # first 3 lines
tail covid.csv        # last 10 lines
wc -l covid.csv       # count lines
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it
Run `cat covid.csv`. Then press Ctrl+C. Now run `head covid.csv` and `tail covid.csv`. Which ones are instant, and why?
:::

`head` and `tail` take several options, and combining them lets you cut out any slice of a file:

```bash
head -n 1 covid.csv                # just the header line
tail -n 2 covid.csv                # the last 2 lines
tail -n +2 covid.csv | head -n 3   # from line 2 on: skips the header
head -n 1000 covid.csv | tail -n 3 # lines 998-1000: first 1000, then last 3
head -c 30 covid.csv               # the first 30 bytes, not lines
```

`wc` counts more than lines, and accepts many files at once:

```bash
wc covid.csv          # lines, words and bytes, in that order
wc -l covid.csv       # lines only
wc -w covid.csv       # words only
wc -c covid.csv       # bytes (the file size)
wc -l *.csv           # one count per file, plus a total
```

`less` is a small program with its own keys, and a few options:

| Key | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| Space / `b` | Page down / page up |
| `g` / `G` | Jump to the start / to the end of the file |
| `/text` +Enter | Search forward for "text" (`n` for next, `N` for previous) |
| `q` | Quit |

```bash
less -N covid.csv     # show line numbers
less -S covid.csv     # no line wrapping (scroll sideways)
head -n 3 covid.csv | cat -n    # cat can number lines too
```

To read a CSV comfortably, line up the columns with `column` (the `|` sends one command's output into the next; it is explained below):

```bash
head covid.csv | column -s, -t    # -s, : fields are separated by commas
```

`tail -f` keeps showing new lines as they are added to a file, which is how you watch a log of a long-running job. To try it, open a second terminal and run the first line, which adds the date to `logfile.txt` every second. Then, in the first terminal, run the second line. Press Ctrl+C in both when done.

```bash
while true; do date >> logfile.txt; sleep 1; done    # terminal 2
tail -f logfile.txt                                  # terminal 1
```

How much space are things taking?

```bash
du -sh .                  # total size of this directory
du -sh ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026   # ...or of any directory you name
du -h -d 1 .              # size of each subdirectory, one level deep
du -sh *                  # size of each item here
du -sh * | sort -h        # ...smallest to largest (sort comes below)
ls -lh                    # sizes of the files in a listing
ls -lhS                   # largest file first (S = sort by size)
ls -lht                   # newest file first (t = sort by time)
ls -lhtr                  # oldest first (r reverses any of these)
ls -R                     # list subfolders too (R = recursive)
df -h                     # free space on every disk
df -h ~                   # free space on the disk holding your home directory
```

And what is in a file?

```bash
file covid.csv            # what kind of file is it? (a file's name can lie)
stat covid.csv            # size, permissions, timestamps (differs on a Mac)
```

How long does a command take? Put `time` in front of it:

```bash
time wc -l covid.csv
```

`real` is the wall-clock time. We'll use `time` all semester to compare methods.

# Redirection and pipes

By default, output goes to the screen. You can send it to a file instead:

```bash
echo "hello" > greeting.txt     # write to a file (replaces its contents!)
echo "again" >> greeting.txt    # append to a file
cat greeting.txt                # two lines
echo "oops" > greeting.txt      # > replaced everything: one line again
cat greeting.txt greeting.txt > twice.txt   # cat joins files: two copies
head -n 1000 covid.csv > sample.csv         # a small file to experiment on
head -n 1 covid.csv > header.txt            # save just the header line
tail -n +2 covid.csv > body.csv             # the data without the header
```

## Standard output, standard error and standard input

Every command has three channels. **Standard input** (stdin, number 0) is where it reads from, the keyboard by default. **Standard output** (stdout, number 1) is where its results go, the screen by default. **Standard error** (stderr, number 2) is where it reports problems, also the screen by default. Error messages travel on their own channel so that they don't end up mixed into your results.

That has a surprising consequence: `>` only redirects stdout. Errors still appear on the screen. To redirect stderr, put its number in front, `2>`:

```bash
ls /nonexistent                      # an error message (stderr)
ls /nonexistent > out.txt            # still on screen: out.txt is empty
ls /nonexistent 2> err.txt           # now the screen is quiet
ls . /nonexistent > out.txt 2> err.txt    # results and errors, separately
ls . /nonexistent > all.txt 2>&1     # both into one file
ls . /nonexistent &> all.txt         # bash shortcut for the line above
ls . /nonexistent 2>> err.txt        # append errors, like >>
```

`2>&1` reads "send channel 2 to wherever channel 1 is going", so it must come *after* the `>` it refers to. Written the other way round, `2>&1 > all.txt`, it sends the errors to the screen instead.

The place to put output you don't want is `/dev/null`, a special file that throws away everything written to it:

```bash
ls . /nonexistent 2>/dev/null        # hide the errors, keep the results
ls . /nonexistent > /dev/null        # hide the results, keep the errors
ls . /nonexistent > /dev/null 2>&1   # hide everything
```

This is what the `find / -name "Rscript" 2>/dev/null` from earlier was doing: hiding the "Permission denied" errors.

Input can be redirected as well, with `<`:

```bash
wc -l covid.csv          # prints the count and the file's name
wc -l < covid.csv        # the file feeds stdin: no name printed
sort < covid.csv | head -n 3     # the same as: sort covid.csv | head -n 3
```

The second form is handy when you want the number alone, for example to use in a script (see below).

Finally, `tee` copies its input to a file and also passes it along, like a T-junction in a pipe:

```bash
head -n 3 covid.csv | tee first3.txt | wc -l    # saves a copy, counts lines
echo "extra" | tee -a first3.txt                # -a appends, like >>
```

## Pipes

The **pipe**, `|`, sends the stdout of one command into the stdin of the next. Each command does one small job, and you chain them:

```bash
grep ",California," covid.csv | head    # rows for California, first 10
grep -c ",California," covid.csv        # count of rows for California
cut -d, -f3 covid.csv | head            # just the 3rd column (the state)
cut -d, -f3 covid.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c   # count rows per state
```

Read the last line left to right: take column 3, drop the header line, sort it, then count identical neighbors. Only stdout goes through a pipe. Errors still reach the screen unless you add `2>&1`:

```bash
ls . /nonexistent | wc -l            # the error is displayed, not counted
ls . /nonexistent 2>&1 | wc -l       # now the error line is counted too
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this matters for big data
Pipes process data as a **stream**: each command reads a line, handles it, and passes it on. None of these commands loads the whole file into memory, which is why they work on files much bigger than your RAM. This is the idea behind the one-pass algorithms we'll study later.
:::

## Searching inside files with grep

`grep` prints the lines of its input that match a pattern. We have used it with a plain word. These examples all search `covid.csv` and show how much one command can do when you add options:

```bash
grep "Alaska" covid.csv | head -n 2     # lines containing Alaska
grep -i "alaska" covid.csv | head -n 2  # -i: ignore upper/lower case
grep -v "Alaska" covid.csv | head -n 2  # -v: lines that do NOT match
grep -c "Alaska" covid.csv              # -c: count matching lines
grep -vc "Alaska" covid.csv             # options combine: count the others
grep -n "Alaska" covid.csv | head -n 2  # -n: show line numbers
grep -m 2 "Alaska" covid.csv            # -m 2: stop after 2 matches
grep -o "2020-03-[0-9][0-9]" covid.csv | head -n 2   # -o: only the match
grep -w "Ada" covid.csv | head -n 2     # -w: whole words only
grep -c "Ada" covid.csv                 # compare: also counts Adams, Adair
grep -A 1 -B 1 -m 1 "Anchorage" covid.csv   # 1 line After, 1 Before
grep -C 2 -m 1 "Anchorage" covid.csv        # -C 2: 2 lines of context
```

You can search for several things at once, and in many files:

```bash
grep -e "Alaska" -e "Hawaii" covid.csv | wc -l    # -e: either pattern
grep -f pats.txt covid.csv | wc -l      # -f: patterns listed in a file
grep -F "." covid.csv | wc -l           # -F: literal text, not a pattern
grep -l "Alaska" sample.csv covid.csv   # -l: only NAMES of files that match
grep -c "Alaska" sample.csv covid.csv   # a count for each file
grep -r "Cook" . | head -n 3            # -r: search every file under here
grep -rl "Cook" .                       # ...and just list which files
grep -r --include="*.csv" -l "Cook" .   # ...but only in csv files
```

(`-f pats.txt` assumes you made that file, for example `printf 'Alaska\nHawaii\n' > pats.txt`.)

`grep` also reports whether it found anything, through its **exit status**, which every command has: 0 means success, anything else means failure. The special variable `$?` holds the status of the last command:

```bash
grep "Alaska" covid.csv > /dev/null; echo $?    # 0: found
grep "Atlantis" covid.csv; echo $?              # 1: not found
grep -q "Alaska" covid.csv; echo $?             # -q: quiet, only the status
```

The exit status is what scripts use to make decisions, as we will see.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `grep` matches anywhere in the line
`grep -c ",Texas," covid.csv` returns 67,497 but Texas has 67,002 rows. The other 495 are the counties named "Texas" in Missouri and in Oklahoma. A plain word can match in the wrong column. The fix is a more precise pattern, which is where regular expressions come in.
:::

## Regular expressions

A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern that describes a set of strings. We have been using the simplest regex, a plain word that matches itself. The real power comes from special characters. A few meet you almost everywhere (R, Python, SQL, text editors), so learning them pays off all semester.

| Pattern | Matches | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `.` | any one character | `Co.k` matches Cook |
| `*` | the previous thing, zero or more times | `Co*k` matches Ck, Cok, Coook |
| `+` | the previous thing, one or more times | `Co+k` matches Cok but not Ck |
| `?` | the previous thing, zero or one times | `Lou?isiana` matches Loisiana and Louisiana |
| `^` | the start of the line | `^2020-03` |
| `$` | the end of the line | `,0$` |
| `[abc]` | one character from the set | `[BC]ook` |
| `[a-z]`, `[0-9]` | one character from a range | `[0-9][0-9]` |
| `[^,]` | one character NOT in the set | `[^,]*` is "a field" |
| `{n}`, `{n,m}` | repeat exactly n, or n to m, times | `[0-9]{5}` |
| <code>a&#124;b</code> | either a or b | <code>Texas&#124;Ohio</code> |
| `( )` | group things together | <code>(Texas&#124;Ohio),</code> |
| `\.` | a literal special character | `\.` is a real dot |

Use `grep -E` ("extended") whenever your pattern has `+ ? | ( ) { }`, otherwise `grep` wants a backslash before each of them. Also put patterns in **single quotes**, so the shell doesn't try to interpret characters like `*`, `$` or `|` before `grep` sees them.

Anchors first, `^` and `$`:

```bash
grep '^2020-03-15' covid.csv | head -n 2       # lines that START with a date
grep -c ',0$' covid.csv                        # lines that END with ,0
grep -c '^2020-0[1-3]' covid.csv               # January to March: a set
grep -Ec '^2020-(03|04)-' covid.csv            # March or April: alternatives
grep -E '^2020-03-1[0-5],' covid.csv | wc -l   # March 10 to 15
grep -x 'date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths' covid.csv   # -x: whole line
```

Repetition and wildcards inside a pattern:

```bash
grep -c 'New .*City' covid.csv          # .* is "anything": New ... City
grep -E 'o+k' covid.csv | head -n 1     # one or more o, then k: Cook
grep -E 'Lou?isiana' covid.csv | head -n 1    # the u is optional
grep -E 'a{2}' covid.csv | head -n 1    # a double "aa"
grep -E ',[0-9]{6,},[0-9]+$' covid.csv | head -n 2    # 100,000 cases or more
```

Precision: the `[^,]*` idiom means "any run of characters that isn't a comma", i.e. one CSV field. It lets you say which column you mean:

```bash
# columns: date , county , state , ...  so the state is after two commas
grep -Ec '^[^,]*,[^,]*,Texas,' covid.csv    # only rows whose STATE is Texas
grep ',Texas,' covid.csv | grep -v '^[^,]*,[^,]*,Texas,' \
  | cut -d, -f2,3 | sort -u
```

The last line shows the 495 impostors. Missing values are easy to find as well. The `fips` column is empty for New York City (the data combines its five boroughs) and for the rows marked "Unknown", so those rows contain two commas in a row:

```bash
grep -c ',,' covid.csv                       # rows with an empty field
grep ',,' covid.csv | head -n 2              # which ones?
grep -E '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2},' covid.csv | wc -l    # valid dates
grep -Ev '^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2},' covid.csv           # the odd ones out
grep -E '^2020-03-15,(New York City|Baldwin),' covid.csv    # a group
grep -E 'Cook,(Illinois|Georgia)' covid.csv | cut -d, -f3 | sort | uniq -c
```

The last two lines of that block show why `grep` is a data-cleaning tool: the fourth finds rows that do *not* look like data (here, the header), which is how you spot problems in a file too big to read. The same idea works with files that have comment lines:

```bash
printf '# settings\nname=x\n\n# more\nn=3\n' > cfg.txt
grep -v '^#' cfg.txt                  # drop the comment lines
grep -c '^$' cfg.txt                  # ^$ is an empty line: count them
grep -v -e '^#' -e '^$' cfg.txt       # drop comments AND blank lines
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Wildcards vs. regular expressions
Both are patterns, and the characters look alike, but they are different languages. In the shell, `*.csv` means "any name ending in .csv". The same thing as a regex is `.*\.csv$`: `.` is any character, `*` repeats it, `\.` is a real dot, and `$` is the end. In particular, the wildcard `*` stands alone, while the regex `*` repeats the thing before it. The shell uses wildcards for file *names*, and `grep` uses regular expressions for text *inside* files.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}

2. How many rows have 5 or more digits in the `cases` column?

## Columns, sorting and counting

`cut` picks columns, `sort` orders lines, and `uniq` collapses repeated lines. They are the backbone of command-line data analysis:

```bash
cut -d, -f1,3 covid.csv | head -n 2     # columns 1 and 3
cut -d, -f2-4 covid.csv | head -n 2     # columns 2 through 4
cut -d, -f4- covid.csv | head -n 2      # column 4 to the end
cut -c1-7 covid.csv | head -n 2         # characters 1-7: not columns at all
cut -c1-7 body.csv | sort | uniq -c     # rows per month (2020-01 etc.)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `cut` doesn't understand quoted fields
`cut -d, -f2` splits at *every* comma, even one inside quotes. For a file with a line `"Smith, John",Boston`, column 2 comes out as ` John"` instead of `Boston`. `covid.csv` has no quoted fields, so we are safe here, but real CSV files often do. Check with `grep -c '"'` first, and use a tool that understands CSV (R, Python, DuckDB) when it matters:

```bash
printf 'name,city\n"Smith, John",Boston\n' > quoted.csv
cut -d, -f2 quoted.csv
```
:::

`sort` has many options:

```bash
printf '10\n9\n100\n' | sort          # 10, 100, 9: text order, not numeric!
printf '10\n9\n100\n' | sort -n       # 9, 10, 100: -n sorts as numbers
printf '10\n9\n100\n' | sort -nr      # 100, 10, 9: -r reverses
printf 'b\nA\na\nB\n' | sort          # a A b B: lower and upper case mix
printf 'b\nA\na\nB\n' | sort -f       # -f: ignore case when comparing
printf '1K\n2G\n3M\n' | sort -h       # 1K, 3M, 2G: -h understands K, M, G
sort -u body.csv | wc -l              # -u: sort, dropping duplicate lines
sort -R body.csv | head -n 3          # -R: shuffle the lines (random rows)
printf 'x\ny\nz\n' | sort -c; echo $? # -c: just check if sorted; 0 = yes
```

To sort a CSV by a column, tell `sort` the separator with `-t` and the column with `-k`. Write the column twice, `-k5,5`, so it sorts on that column alone and not everything after it:

```bash
sort -t, -k5,5 -n -r body.csv | head -n 3   # largest case counts, any county
sort -t, -k3,3 -k5,5nr body.csv | head -n 3 # state, then cases (high to low)
sort -t, -k4,4 -u body.csv | wc -l          # one row per distinct fips code
```

`uniq` removes repeated lines, but only repeated *neighbors*, which is why it almost always follows a `sort`:

```bash
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | uniq               # a b a c: neighbors only
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | sort | uniq        # a b c
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | sort | uniq -c     # with counts: 3 a, 1 b, 1 c
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | sort | uniq -d     # -d: only lines that repeat
printf 'a\nb\na\na\nc\n' | sort | uniq -u     # -u: lines that appear once
printf 'a\nA\n' | sort | uniq -ic             # -i: ignore case
```

Put them together and you can answer real questions about a file with 885,000 rows in a few seconds:

```bash
cut -d, -f3 body.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5   # top 5 states
cut -d, -f3 body.csv | sort -u | wc -l           # how many distinct "states"?
cut -d, -f2,3 body.csv | sort -u | wc -l         # distinct county-state pairs
cut -d, -f1 body.csv | sort -u | head -n 1       # the first date in the file
grep -E ',(Texas|Ohio),' body.csv | cut -d, -f1,2,5 | head -n 2
```

The pattern `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` is the single most useful idiom here: *count how often each value occurs, and show the most common first*. Notice that `cut -d, -f3 | sort -u | wc -l` says 55, not 50: the file includes DC, Puerto Rico, Guam and other territories.

::: {.callout-tip}

2. Which county has the largest number of deaths, ever? (Hint: `sort` by column 6.)
3. How many distinct county names are there? Why is it different from the number of distinct (county, state) pairs?

# Shell scripts

A **script** is a text file of commands that the shell runs one after another. Anything you type at the prompt, you can save in a script and rerun. Before we write one, we need a few pieces of the shell's own language.

## Variables and quoting

```bash
name="Ada"                  # make a variable: NO spaces around the =
echo $name                  # use it with a $
echo "Hello, $name"         # inside double quotes, $name is replaced
echo 'Hello, $name'         # inside single quotes, nothing is replaced
echo "Today is $(date +%F)" # $(...) runs a command and pastes in its output
echo "files here: $(ls | wc -l)"
echo "$(wc -l < covid.csv) rows"
```

Quotes also protect spaces. A name with a space is two words to the shell unless you quote it:

```bash
touch "my file.txt"         # one file with a space in its name
ls my file.txt              # error: looks for files "my" and "file.txt"
ls "my file.txt"            # works
ls my\ file.txt             # works: a backslash escapes the space
```

The habit to build: **put double quotes around every variable** (`"$name"`, `"$file"`), because a filename with a space will otherwise break your script.

## Chaining commands and exit status

Recall that every command ends with an exit status: 0 for success, anything else for failure. The shell can chain commands based on it:

```bash
echo a; echo b                    # ; runs both, whatever happens
mkdir results && cd results       # && : second only if the first worked
cd /nonexistent && echo "arrived" # the echo never runs
false || echo "first one failed"  # || : second only if first failed
grep -q "Alaska" covid.csv && echo "found it"
grep -q "Atlantis" covid.csv || echo "not there"
true; echo $?                     # 0
false; echo $?                    # 1
```

## Your first script

Let's write a script that counts the rows for one state. The next command creates the file `count_state.sh` with the text between the two `EOF` lines (this is a "here document", a way to type a file into the terminal; you could equally write the file with `vi`):

```bash
cat > count_state.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Usage: ./count_state.sh FILE STATE
if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then
  echo "usage: $0 FILE STATE" >&2
  exit 1
fi
file=$1
state=$2
n=$(grep -Ec "^[^,]*,[^,]*,$state," "$file")
echo "$state has $n rows in $file"
EOF
```

What is in it:

- `#!/usr/bin/env bash` on the first line (the "shebang") says which program should run the file.
- Lines starting with `#` are comments.
- `$1`, `$2`, ... are the **arguments** you type after the script's name. `$#` is how many there are, `$0` is the script's name, and `"$@"` is all of them.
- `if [ ... ]; then ... fi` runs commands only when a test is true. Here: "if there are fewer than 2 arguments". The spaces inside `[ ]` are required.
- `>&2` sends the message to stderr, and `exit 1` stops with a failure status.
- Everything else is commands you already know.

There are two ways to run it:

```bash
bash count_state.sh covid.csv Texas     # run it through bash explicitly
./count_state.sh covid.csv Texas        # error: Permission denied
ls -l count_state.sh                    # no x: not executable
chmod +x count_state.sh                 # add execute permission (x)
ls -l count_state.sh                    # -rwxr-xr-x: now it has x
./count_state.sh covid.csv Texas        # works
count_state.sh covid.csv Texas          # error: command not found
./count_state.sh covid.csv              # too few arguments: prints the usage
echo $?                                 # 1: the script's exit status
./count_state.sh covid.csv Utah 2>/dev/null   # hide any error messages
```

The `./` means "the file in this directory". Without it, the shell looks for the name only in the directories of your `PATH` (which we met earlier), and the current directory isn't among them. See the last section below for how to put your scripts on the `PATH`.

## Loops and tests

A **for loop** repeats commands for every item in a list. This is how you run the same analysis on many states, files or months:

```bash
for i in 1 2 3; do echo "round $i"; done          # a fixed list
for i in $(seq 1 5); do echo "n=$i"; done         # seq makes a sequence
for i in {1..5}; do echo "n=$i"; done             # a shortcut for the same
for s in Texas Ohio Utah; do                      # a loop can span lines
  echo "$s: $(grep -Ec "^[^,]*,[^,]*,$s," covid.csv)"
done
for m in 01 02 03; do echo "$m $(grep -c "^2020-$m" covid.csv)"; done
for s in Texas Ohio Utah; do                      # a file for each state
  grep -E "^[^,]*,[^,]*,$s," covid.csv > "$s.csv"
done
for f in *.csv; do echo "$f has $(wc -l < "$f") lines"; done   # all csv files
head -n 2 covid.csv | while read line; do echo "got: $line"; done
```

The `if` test can check many things. The brackets `[ ... ]` are really a command called `test`, and the useful ones are:

| Test | True when |
|------|-----------|
| `[ -f covid.csv ]` | the file exists |
| `[ -d results ]` | the directory exists |
| `[ -s covid.csv ]` | the file exists and is not empty |
| `[ "$a" = "$b" ]` | the two strings are equal |
| `[ $n -gt 5 ]` | the number is greater than 5 (also `-lt -ge -le -eq -ne`) |
| `[ ! -f covid.csv ]` | the test inside is NOT true |

```bash
if [ -f covid.csv ]; then echo "exists"; else echo "missing"; fi
[ -s Utah.csv ] && echo "Utah.csv has data"
n=7; if [ $n -gt 5 ]; then echo "big"; fi
if grep -q "Utah" covid.csv; then echo "Utah is in the file"; fi
if [ ! -d results ]; then mkdir results; fi
```

The last line of the block above shows how `if` works with any command, not just `[ ]`: it asks "did this command succeed (exit status 0)?" That is also why `grep -q` exists.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it
Write a script `top_states.sh` that takes a file and a number N, and prints the N states with the most rows. Use `$1` and `$2`, and the pipeline from the sorting section (`head -n "$2"`). Then make it print a usage message and exit if the file does not exist.
:::

## Your own commands: `PATH`, `export` and `alias`

The `PATH` is a list of directories. When you type a command name, the shell looks for it in each of them. A good place for your own scripts is a `bin` folder in your home directory:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/bin                       # a folder for your own programs
cp count_state.sh ~/bin/             # put the script there
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"        # add ~/bin to the front of the PATH
which count_state.sh                 # now the shell finds it...
count_state.sh covid.csv Utah        # ...and it runs from anywhere
```

`export` makes a variable available to the programs you start, and the `PATH` change lasts only as long as this terminal window. To make it permanent, add the line to the file that the shell reads whenever it starts, `~/.bashrc` on Ubuntu (`~/.zshrc` on a Mac). An **alias** is a shortcut for a longer command, and it belongs in the same file:

```bash
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc    # for every new terminal
echo "alias ll='ls -lha'" >> ~/.bashrc               # a shortcut: ll
source ~/.bashrc                    # read the file now, instead of reopening
type ll                             # what kind of name is ll?
```

# Processes

Every running program is a **process** with an ID number (PID).

```bash
ps                    # your processes in this terminal
ps aux | head         # every process on the machine
ps -u $USER | head    # just your processes, from every terminal
ps aux | grep python  # find a process by name (grep filters the list)
pgrep -l python       # the same, simpler: PID and name of matches
htop                  # live view of CPU and memory (q quits)
top                   # the older version, available everywhere
```

How big is the machine you are on? This matters for deciding how much data fits and how many things can run in parallel:

```bash
nproc                 # number of CPU cores (on a Mac: sysctl -n hw.ncpu)
free -h                # memory used and free (Linux only)
uptime                # how long it has been up, and the recent load average
```

**Demo: watch a process eat CPU.** Run this in one terminal, and `htop` in another:

```bash
yes > /dev/null &     # a useless program that uses 100% of one core
```

The `&` runs it in the **background**, so you get your prompt back. Now manage it:

```bash
jobs                  # list background jobs in this terminal
fg                    # bring it to the foreground (then Ctrl+C stops it)
kill %1               # or: stop background job number 1
pkill yes             # or: stop every process named yes
kill 12345            # or: stop a process by its PID
kill -9 12345         # last resort: force it
```

Forgot the `&`? You can still get your prompt back. Run something slow in the foreground, such as `sleep 300`, and then:

```bash
# press Ctrl+Z   # pauses the running command and gives you the prompt back
bg               # lets the paused command continue, in the background
jobs             # it is listed as Running
fg               # bring it back to the foreground; Ctrl+C then stops it
```

A job started with `&` belongs to your terminal window and stops when you close it. For something long, like a model fit on a remote server, use `nohup` ("no hang-up"), which keeps it alive after you log out. It uses the redirections from earlier to save the output:

```bash
nohup python3 long_job.py > out.log 2>&1 &    # survives logging out
tail -f out.log                               # check on it whenever you like
```

**Demo: watch a process use memory.** With `htop` open, and `free -h` run before, during and after, run:

```bash
python3 -c "x = 'a' * 10**9; input('Press Enter to quit')"
```

Watch the memory bar jump by about 1 GB (the `used` column of `free -h` does too). Press Enter and watch it drop. This is what "fits in RAM" means in practice.

# Wrap-up

## Cheat sheet

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `pwd`, `ls`, `cd` | Where am I, what's here, go somewhere |
| `mkdir`, `touch` | Make a directory, make an empty file |
| `cp`, `mv`, `rm` | Copy, move/rename, delete (permanently!) |
| `*`, `?`, `[...]` | Wildcards: match many file names at once |
| `find` | Search for files by name, size, age, type, and act on them |
| `chmod`, `sudo` | Change permissions, run as administrator |
| `vi` | Edit files in the terminal |
| `cat`, `less`, `column` | Print a file, scroll through a file, line up columns |
| `head`, `tail`, `wc` | First lines, last lines, count lines/words/bytes |
| `du`, `df`, `file`, `stat` | Space used, free space, what a file is |
| `time` | How long a command takes |
| `>`, `>>`, `2>`, `<`, `tee` | Write, append, send errors, read input, copy a stream |
| <code>&#124;</code> | Pipe: stdout of one command into stdin of the next |
| `grep -i -v -c -n -w -o -E -r -l` | Find lines that match a pattern or regular expression |
| `cut`, `sort`, `uniq` | Pick columns, sort lines (`-n`, `-r`, `-k`), count duplicates |
| `$?`, `&&`, <code>&#124;&#124;</code> | Exit status, "then", "otherwise" |
| `$var`, `$(cmd)`, `for`, `if` | Variables, command output, loops, tests |
| `PATH`, `export`, `alias`, `source` | Where programs are found, settings, shortcuts, reload |
| `ps`, `htop`, `top`, `free`, `nproc` | See running processes, memory and cores |
| `&`, `jobs`, `fg`, `bg`, `kill`, `nohup` | Background, list, foreground, stop, survive logout |
| `man`, `--help` | Get help |

### Regular expression building blocks

| Pattern | Matches |
|---------|---------|
| `.` `*` `+` `?` | any one character; repeat 0+, 1+, 0 or 1 times |
| `^` `$` | start of line, end of line |
| `[abc]` `[0-9]` `[^,]` | one of a set, one of a range, one NOT in the set |
| `{3}` `{2,5}` | repeat exactly 3 times, 2 to 5 times |
| <code>(a&#124;b)</code> | a group with alternatives |
| `\.` | a literal special character |

## Check yourself

These are the kinds of questions you should be able to answer on an exam, without a computer or AI.

1. What's the difference between an absolute and a relative path? Give an example of each.
2. You're in `~/bigdata/lec01`. What does `cd ../..` do?
3. What's the difference between `>` and `>>`?
4. You opened a file in `vi` and typed text you don't want to keep. How do you get out without saving?
5. Why is `head` instant on a 10 GB file while `cat` is not?
6. What does `cut -d, -f3 covid.csv | sort | uniq -c` produce?
7. Your laptop's fan is suddenly loud. How do you find out which process is responsible, and how do you stop it?
8. Why is `rm -r *` dangerous?
9. `ls /nonexistent > out.txt` still prints an error. Why? Write a command that puts the normal output in `out.txt` and the errors in `err.txt`.
10. What is the difference between `2>&1 > all.txt` and `> all.txt 2>&1`?
11. What does `grep -v '^#' file` print? What does `grep -c '^$' file` count?
12. Write a `grep` that matches lines of `covid.csv` whose *state* is Ohio (and not a county named Ohio). Why doesn't `grep ",Ohio,"` do it?
13. What does `printf '10\n9\n100\n' | sort` print? How do you get numeric order?
14. Write a pipeline that prints the ten most common county names in `covid.csv`.
15. Why is `uniq` almost always used after `sort`?
16. `cut -d, -f2` on the line `"Smith, John",Boston` gives ` John"`. Why?
17. What is the difference between `cmd1; cmd2`, `cmd1 && cmd2` and `cmd1 || cmd2`?
18. You wrote `report.sh` and ran `report.sh`. You get "command not found". Give two ways to run it.
19. What do `$1`, `$#` and `$?` mean?
20. How is a job started with `&` different from one started with `nohup`?
